label: fact-check
system: You fact-check the surprise claims planned for a short explainer video, before its narration is written. For each claim: verdict "keep" if the research notes support it as written; "reword" if the true version is close (give the claim with exactly the wording and numbers the sources support, e.g. "over 600 gallons" for a rounded figure, "New England" instead of a wrong state); "drop" if it is false, unsupported or a myth. Judge ONLY from the research notes (a claim they do not support is dropped) and copy the source URLs from them (url and title) for keep and reword. Write each claim the way the narrator will say it: no abbreviations (never "US", "U.S." or "USA": "American", "in America"; an agency without the country: "the Department of Energy", "the Army Corps of Engineers").

Topic: septic tank
Claims (index: claim | suggested search):
0: A typical household septic tank holds about 1,000 gallons | typical household septic tank size 1000 gallons
1: In a septic tank solids settle to the bottom as sludge while fats, oil and grease float to the top as scum | EPA how septic systems work sludge scum

Research notes (from 4 web searches):
I searched every claim.

**Claim 0: a typical household septic tank holds about 1,000 gallons. Supported in a corrected form.**
- Encyclopedia.com (Septic Tank entry): "an average tank holds 1,000 gal (3,790 l) of liquid." URL: https://www.encyclopedia.com/reference/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/septic-tank
- Sizing guides: "Most building codes require a minimum 1,000-gallon septic tank for a 3-bedroom home"; others give 1,250 gallons for 3 bedrooms; codes vary. URL: https://hakaru.io/guides/septic-tank-size-calculator-guide
- Corrected wording: "A family tank often holds around 1,000 gallons."

**Claim 1: solids settle as sludge, fats, oil and grease float as scum. Supported as written.**
- EPA, How your septic system works: wastewater separates; solids settle to the bottom forming sludge, oil and grease float to the top as scum, the middle liquid goes to the drainfield. URL: https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-your-septic-system-works
- LA County Public Health, How a septic system works: same three layers. URL: https://admin.publichealth.lacounty.gov/eh/docs/business/how-septic-system-works.pdf

**Claim 2: pumped every 3 to 5 years. Supported as written.**
- Cornell Cooperative Extension, reproducing the EPA homeowner guide: "Generally, sludge and scum should be pumped from the septic tank every three to five years, depending on the size of the tank and the amount and composition of wastewater." URL: https://www.css.cornell.edu/cwmi/waterquality/septic/CCEWQ-YourSepticSystem-Print.pdf
- EPA also says inspect about every three years. URL: https://www.epa.gov/septic/how-your-septic-system-works

**Claim 3: more than one in five US homes use a septic system. Supported in a corrected form.**
- EPA SepticSmart Homeowners: "One in five U.S. homes have septic systems." URL: https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/septic/septicsmart-homeowners_.html
- Corrected wording: "About one in five US homes uses a septic system."

Extra searches: 1,000 gallons is the usual minimum for a 3-bedroom home in most US codes (some 1,250) URL: https://www.thedonutwhole.com/how-many-bedrooms-can-a-1000-gallon-septic-tank-handle/ ; EPA blog: "more than one-in-five households in the United States depend on septic systems ... more than 26 million homes" URL: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/web/20161225055203/https://blog.epa.gov/blog/tag/septic-smart-week
